Title: Dummy Health Checks
QuestionDetail: Route 53's health checkers send a fixed-size table of results even when almost no health checks are configured. Why pad it with dummy entries?
AnswerDetails: Padding keeps network load and aggregator work identical no matter how many checks a customer has configured. The system's busiest day looks exactly like its quietest one, which removes a large source of variance.
OptionA: To keep network load and aggregator work constant
OptionB: To test spare capacity on a schedule
OptionC: To keep a backup in case real checks fail
OptionD: To compress better over the wire

Title: Caches Are Not Free
QuestionDetail: Caching looks anti-fragile — it speeds things up under load. What makes it a risky foundation for a critical system?
AnswerDetails: A cache has two modes, warm and empty, and the empty mode arrives exactly when you can least afford it. A cold cache after a restart or a flush can push load onto the backend at the worst moment and turn a small problem into a cascading failure.
OptionA: It has two very different operating modes
OptionD: It is hard to configure correctly

Title: Configuration by S3, Not Workflow
QuestionDetail: AWS Hyperplane distributes Network Load Balancer configuration as full config files in S3 rather than as a stream of change events through a workflow system. What does that buy?
AnswerDetails: Every node fetches and applies the whole configuration on a regular cycle, so processing time does not depend on how many changes happened. A workflow system would slow down precisely during the large, unusual change bursts you most need it to survive.
OptionA: Processing time stays the same no matter how many changes occurred

Title: Sized for the Worst Day
QuestionDetail: Hyperplane's configuration file is sized to its maximum from day one, with unused slots left empty. Why start at full size?
AnswerDetails: Fixed size means fixed work. A file that grows with real usage would make every read, transfer and apply step slower over time and would behave differently under load than it did in testing.
OptionC: To keep the work of each cycle constant

Title: Self-Healing by Default
QuestionDetail: Why do constant-work designs tend to be self-healing, where workflow-driven systems need explicit repair logic?
AnswerDetails: Each cycle re-applies the entire desired state from scratch, so a corrupted or missed update is simply overwritten on the next pass. Nothing accumulates in a backlog and there is no separate repair path that could itself be broken.
OptionB: They carry state forward between cycles
OptionD: They start from a clean slate every cycle

Title: What Constant Work Is Not
QuestionDetail: Which of these is NOT a property of a constant-work system?
AnswerDetails: Constant-work systems avoid scaling with load and avoid modes, and when they do vary they do less work under stress, not more. Caching is the classic counter-example: it appears to help under load but introduces exactly the modes the pattern is trying to eliminate.
OptionA: It gets faster by caching hot results
OptionB: It does not speed up or slow down with load
OptionC: It has no distinct operating modes
OptionD: Under stress it may do less work, never more
